content: Urinary hesitancy can affect individuals of all ages and both sexes, but it is most commonly observed in older men with an enlarged prostate gland. This condition typically develops gradually over time, and many individuals may not notice it until they experience urinary retention, where they are unable to urinate, leading to bladder swelling and discomfort. Nearly all older men experience some degree of difficulty with dribbling, initiating urination, or having a weaker urine stream. Causes of Urinary Hesitancy: Urinary hesitancy can result from various factors, including: Certain medications, such as some cold remedies, nasal decongestants, tricyclic antidepressants, and anticholinergic drugs used for incontinence. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate). Prostatitis, which is inflammation or infection of the prostate gland. Disorders of the nervous system. Postoperative urinary retention following recent surgery. Urethral strictures caused by scar tissue. Shy or bashful bladder syndrome, where individuals are unable to urinate in the presence of others. Urinary tract infections. Home Care Recommendations: Keep track of your urination patterns and report them to your doctor. Apply heat to the lower abdomen, specifically below the belly button and above the pubic bone, where the bladder is located. Heat can help relax the muscles and facilitate urination. Massage or apply gentle pressure over the bladder to stimulate emptying. Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids. If an infection is suspected, antibiotics prescribed by a doctor will be necessary. Symptoms of a possible infection include burning or pain during urination, frequent urination, cloudy urine, and a strong, sudden urge to urinate. Be mindful of any medications or supplements you are taking, as they may contribute to urinary hesitancy. When to Contact a Medical Professional: You should contact your doctor if you experience urinary hesitancy, dribbling, or a weak urine stream and have not been evaluated for these symptoms. Seek immediate medical attention if: You have a fever, vomiting, side or back pain, shaking chills, or are passing very little urine over 1 to 2 days. You notice blood in your urine, cloudy urine, frequent or urgent urination, or discharge from the penis or vagina. You are completely unable to pass urine. What to Expect During a Medical Evaluation: Your doctor will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination, focusing on the pelvis, rectum, abdomen, and lower back. Questions you may be asked include: How long have you had difficulty starting your urine flow? Did the problem develop gradually or suddenly? Is it worse in the morning or at night? Has the force of your urine stream decreased? Do you experience dribbling or uncontrollable urine leakage? Does anything, such as heat or abdominal massage, help alleviate the symptoms? Does anything worsen the hesitancy? Do you have other symptoms, such as fever, pain or burning during urination, cloudy or bloody urine, or back or side pain? Do you have a history of bladder or kidney infections, prostate enlargement or infection, or nervous system disorders? Have you recently undergone any pelvic or bladder surgery, injury, or procedures? What medications, including over-the-counter drugs, are you currently taking? Diagnostic Tests: The following tests may be performed to determine the cause of urinary hesitancy: Bladder catheterization to measure residual urine volume and obtain a urine sample for culture. Cystometrography to assess bladder function. Transrectal ultrasound of the prostate, similar to a transvaginal ultrasound. Urethral swab for culture. Urinalysis and urine culture. Voiding cystourethrogram to evaluate the bladder and urethra during urination. Treatment Options: Treatment for urinary hesitancy depends on the underlying cause. Medications such as alpha-blockers are often effective in relieving symptoms. If a bacterial infection is present, antibiotics will be prescribed. In cases of prostate obstruction, surgical intervention, such as transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), may be necessary.
